title: A frown that the Quran chose to record.
subtitle: Small reactions are seen and weighed

row.title: just a face
sub: he could not even see it

row.title: a real turning away
sub: Allah saw it and named it

then: The Prophet ﷺ was speaking with one of the great leaders of Quraysh, hoping he would accept Islam. Ibn Umm Maktum, a blind man and an early Muslim, came asking about the faith. {trap}The Prophet ﷺ frowned and turned toward the leader.{/trap} The surah opens by naming that moment.
now: You are on a call with an important client when your younger brother walks in with a question. You do not say anything rude. You just give him a look and turn your chair. {idea}That small turn is a choice too.{/idea}
old: A look on my face is not really an action.
new: Allah counts even the frown and the turned shoulder.
try: Today, when someone interrupts you, turn your face fully toward them for a moment before answering.

title: The reason given: the blind man came.
subtitle: The person who seemed like an interruption
then: Aishah reported that Ibn Umm Maktum came saying, {reward}guide me{/reward}, while a leader of the idolaters sat with the Prophet ﷺ. The verse names him only as the blind man. {idea}The one who could not see is the one the surah defends.{/idea}
now: The intern who asks a basic question during the important meeting. The elderly neighbour who calls when you are rushing out. The child who tugs your sleeve. {trap}They feel like interruptions.{/trap} Sometimes they are the reason you are there.
old: This person is getting in the way of something important.
new: The person in front of me, asking sincerely, may be the important thing.
try: Notice the next person you label as an interruption today, and give them two full minutes.

title: You cannot see who is about to grow.
subtitle: Hidden potential in the overlooked person
then: Allah asks the Prophet ﷺ how he could know. Ibn Kathir explains it means the man {reward}may attain purification and cleanliness in his soul.{/reward} The leader seemed the bigger prize, but {idea}the real growth was waiting in the quiet seeker.{/idea}
now: You coach a youth team and give your attention to the two kids who already play well. The shy one in the back asks how to hold the ball. {idea}You have no idea what that question might turn into.{/idea}
old: I can judge who will benefit most from my time.
new: I cannot see who is about to change. Allah can.
try: Answer one question today from someone you would usually skip, as carefully as you would for anyone.

title: One reminder might have changed his life.
subtitle: The value of a word given to the willing
then: The verse continues the question: perhaps he would be reminded, and the reminder would help him. Ibn Kathir says it means {reward}he may receive admonition and abstain from the forbidden.{/reward} {idea}He came ready to listen.{/idea}
now: Your friend messages late at night: I think I want to pray again, where do I start? You are tired and reply with a thumbs up. {idea}A short honest answer now might be the one that sticks.{/idea}
old: A quick answer to a small question does not matter much.
new: A reminder given to someone who asked can change their whole path.
try: Reply properly to one question about faith or life that you have been leaving on read.

title: The man who felt he needed nothing.
subtitle: Self-sufficiency as a closed door
then: The leader sitting with the Prophet ﷺ was one of the great men of Quraysh. Ibn Kathir calls him the one who {trap}thinks himself self-sufficient.{/trap} He had wealth and status, and so felt no need for what was being offered.
now: You have the salary, the car, the healthy parents. When someone mentions Allah, you nod politely and check your phone. {trap}Nothing is wrong, so nothing feels needed.{/trap} That feeling is the thing the verse names.
old: I am doing fine, so I do not really need reminders.
new: Feeling I need nothing is exactly what closes me to guidance.
try: Make one honest dua today that starts with: O Allah, I need You for this.

title: Attention flowed toward the one who did not want it.
subtitle: Where our attention naturally goes
then: Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: {idea}you face the rich person so that perhaps he may be guided.{/idea} The Prophet's ﷺ hope was good, yet Allah pointed out that the eager attention was going to the one who showed no need.
now: At the family gathering you spend the evening impressing the uncle with connections. Your quiet cousin, who wanted to talk about something hard, leaves early. {trap}Our attention follows status without asking us.{/trap}
old: It makes sense to focus on the people who can do the most.
new: My attention should follow sincerity, not status.
try: At your next gathering, seek out the person who is sitting alone and talk with them first.

title: His refusal is not your burden.
subtitle: You deliver; guidance belongs to Allah
then: Ibn Kathir reads it as: {idea}you are not responsible for him if he does not attain purification.{/idea} Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to warn the noble and the weak equally, and then Allah guides whomever He chooses.
now: You keep chasing one relative with long messages, hoping to change their mind, while your own kids get your leftover patience. {idea}Your job is to say it well and kindly. The result is not yours to carry.{/idea}
old: If they do not change, it means I failed.
new: I am asked to convey and be fair. Guidance is in Allah's hands.
try: Let go of one argument you keep trying to win, and make dua for that person instead.

title: He came running, by his own will.
subtitle: The effort of the one who seeks
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {reward}he is seeking you and he comes to you so that he may be guided by what you say.{/reward} A blind man in Makkah had made his way to the Prophet ﷺ. {idea}No one sent him. He came.{/idea}
now: A new colleague keeps showing up early to ask how things work. A teenager at the masjid stays behind after the talk. {reward}Their effort is a kind of knocking.{/reward} It is easy to miss when you are busy.
old: People who keep asking are just being needy.
new: Someone who comes to me striving deserves my best attention.
try: Thank one person today for coming to you with a question, then answer it fully.

title: He came with fear of Allah in his heart.
subtitle: The inner state behind the question
then: The verse describes Ibn Umm Maktum as one who {idea}fears{/idea} while he strives toward the Prophet ﷺ. The leader felt self-sufficient. The blind man came afraid for his soul. {reward}Allah looked at the heart, not the rank.{/reward}
now: Two people message you about a lecture. One wants to argue for fun. One writes, I am scared I am getting this wrong. {idea}The second message carries something precious.{/idea} It deserves a slower reply.
old: I judge people mostly by how important they look.
new: The fear of Allah in someone's heart is what makes them weighty.
try: Before you reply to someone today, ask yourself what they might be feeling, not who they are.

title: Too busy for the one who truly came.
subtitle: Distraction from what matters most
then: Ibn Kathir sums it up in two words: {trap}you are too busy.{/trap} Here Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ not to single anyone out. {idea}The warning is for the noble and the weak, the rich and the poor, the young and the old alike.{/idea}
now: Your daughter is telling you about her day while you answer emails. You say mm-hm three times. {trap}You were there, but not with her.{/trap} The verse asks who you were really busy with.
old: I can half-listen now and give full attention later.
new: Being too busy for a sincere person is a loss I may not get back.
try: Put your phone face down for one conversation today and listen until the person is finished.

title: No. This is a reminder, not a privilege.
subtitle: The message is for everyone equally
then: The surah turns with a firm {trap}No!{/trap} Ibn Kathir says the reminder refers to this surah, or to {idea}the advice of conveying knowledge equally among people, whether noble or low class.{/idea} Qatadah and As-Suddi said it means the Quran.
now: Your study circle quietly becomes a club for the articulate ones. The cleaner at your office never gets invited. {idea}The Quran was never meant to have a guest list.{/idea}
old: Some people are more suited to religious knowledge than others.
new: The reminder belongs equally to everyone who will listen.
try: Share one verse or good word today with someone you would not normally talk to about faith.

title: Whoever wants it can take it.
subtitle: The door is open, the choice is yours
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {reward}whoever wills, he remembers Allah in all of his affairs.{/reward} After the scene with the chief and the blind man, the point is clear. {idea}No one is pushed in and no one is kept out.{/idea}
now: You keep waiting to feel more qualified, more pious, less busy before you open the Quran. {idea}The verse only asks one thing: do you want it?{/idea} The app is already on your phone.
old: I am not the kind of person who is really religious.
new: The reminder is open to me the moment I choose it.
try: Read one page of Quran today, at whatever pace you can.

title: Written on pages held in honor.
subtitle: The dignity of what you are reading
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}all of the Quran is in honored pages, meaning respected and revered.{/reward} The leader of Quraysh did not need to accept it for it to matter. {idea}Its honor came from Allah, not from any audience.{/idea}
now: You hesitate to mention the Quran at work because it might seem uncool. {idea}Its worth does not rise or fall with anyone's reaction in the break room.{/idea} It was honored before you opened it.
old: The message matters more when important people accept it.
new: The Quran is honored by Allah, whoever accepts or ignores it.
try: Handle your Quran or open the app today with one moment of deliberate respect before reading.

title: Raised high and kept pure.
subtitle: Nothing added, nothing missing
then: Ibn Kathir explains the two words: exalted means {reward}elevated in status{/reward}, and purified means {idea}free from impurity, additions and deficiency.{/idea} This is the reminder the proud chief turned away from.
now: Your feed is full of edited clips, rumors, and posts that change every hour. {idea}Then there is one text that has not been bent.{/idea} You can open it at the bus stop.
old: Everything I read is shaped by someone's agenda.
new: The Quran is kept high and clean, a steady thing in a noisy world.
try: Swap five minutes of scrolling today for five minutes with the Quran.

title: Carried down by angel ambassadors.
subtitle: The messengers who bring the revelation
then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said the Safarah {idea}are the angels.{/idea} Al-Bukhari explained that they descend with Allah's revelation {reward}like the ambassador who rectifies matters between people.{/reward}
now: You pass on a forwarded message without checking it. A rumour travels through your office in a day. {idea}The Quran came through carriers who never twisted a word.{/idea} It asks you to be a careful carrier too.
old: How a message reaches me does not really matter.
new: The Quran reached me through honored hands, and I can pass it on with the same care.
try: Before forwarding anything today, check it first, or do not send it.

title: Noble carriers, and you can stand with them.
subtitle: The reciter's company with the angels
then: Ibn Kathir says the angels are {reward}noble and honorable{/reward}, righteous and pure in deeds. He cites the hadith from Aishah: the one who recites the Quran well {idea}will be with the noble, righteous ambassador angels{/idea}, and the one who struggles with it gets two rewards.
now: You stumble over the Arabic at night, sounding out each letter, and feel embarrassed. {reward}That stumbling earns double.{/reward} The fluent reciter at the masjid and you are both in good company.
old: My recitation is too poor to count for much.
new: Struggling through the Quran carries its own double reward.
try: Recite one short surah aloud today, slowly, even if you stumble.

title: How ungrateful man can be.
subtitle: Denial without any real argument
then: Ibn Abbas explained the opening word as a curse on man. Abu Malik said it refers to {trap}the rejecting type, who denies without any supporting argument{/trap}, simply because the Resurrection seems farfetched to him. The verses that follow answer that doubt.
now: You wake up breathing, eat breakfast you did not grow, and drive to work on a body you did not design. {trap}Gratitude can go missing in a normal morning.{/trap} The verse is a hard knock on that forgetfulness.
old: I am not ungrateful, I just do not think about it much.
new: Not thinking about where everything came from is its own kind of ingratitude.
try: Name three things you did not make but used before noon today, and thank Allah for each.

title: Ask yourself what you were made from.
subtitle: A question that shrinks arrogance
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah explains here {idea}how He created him from something despised{/idea}, and that {reward}He is able to bring him back to life just as He created him initially.{/reward} The question is meant to stop the denier in his tracks.
now: You scroll past a baby scan photo in the family group chat. A few weeks ago that child was almost nothing. {idea}So were you.{/idea} Pride gets quieter when you remember the start.
old: I have always been more or less who I am now.
new: I began as almost nothing, and the One who made me can make me again.
try: Look at a baby photo of yourself today and say a quiet alhamdulillah.

title: From a drop, with everything measured out.
subtitle: Your life was planned from its first moment
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah created man from a drop and then set him in proportion, meaning {idea}He decreed his life span, his sustenance, his deeds{/idea}, and whether he would be miserable or happy.
now: You lie awake doing salary maths, worried the provision will run out. {reward}Your provision was measured before you were born.{/reward} Your job is the effort. The amount is already written.
old: Everything in my life depends on my own planning.
new: My span and provision were set by Allah. My part is how I use them.
try: Tonight, before sleeping, hand one money worry to Allah in a short dua and leave it there.

title: Then He made the way easy for you.
subtitle: Birth, and the path laid clear
then: Ibn Abbas said it means {reward}He made his coming out of his mother's belly easy for him.{/reward} Mujahid linked it to 76:3, that Allah guided man on the path, grateful or ungrateful. Ibn Kathir calls this second view {idea}the most correct, and Allah knows best.{/idea}
now: You know where the prayer times are on your phone. You know which friend drags you down. {idea}Most of the path is already clear.{/idea} What is left is whether you walk it.
old: I would do better if the right way were clearer.
new: Allah has already made the way plain. The choice to walk it is mine.
try: Pick one good thing you already know you should do, and do it once today.

title: Then death, and a place in the earth.
subtitle: The grave is part of the honor
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}after creating man, Allah causes him to die and makes him the inhabitant of a grave.{/idea} Creation, the easy path, then death. The sequence keeps moving because {reward}the story is not finished.{/reward}
now: You stand at a funeral in the rain, watching the earth go back over someone you knew. You check your phone in the car afterwards. {idea}That grave is a waypoint, not a full stop.{/idea}
old: Death is the end of the story and best not thought about.
new: Death and the grave are a stage Allah arranged, with more to come.
try: Visit a grave, or simply make dua today for one person you have lost.

title: When He wills, He raises you again.
subtitle: Resurrection as the next step
then: Ibn Kathir says this is called {idea}al-Ba'th and an-Nushur{/idea}, the resurrection. He cites 30:20 and 2:259, and the hadith in the Two Sahihs that every human decays except the tailbone, {reward}from which he will be reconstructed.{/reward}
now: You plant a seed in a pot on the windowsill and forget it. A week later there is green. {idea}Something that looked gone came back.{/idea} The verse asks you to take that seriously about yourself.
old: Being brought back after death is hard to believe.
new: The One who made me from nothing will raise me when He wills.
try: Say this once today with meaning: I will be raised, so let me live like it.

title: No, he has not done what he was told.
subtitle: The gap between claim and duty

row.title: Ibn Jarir
sub: man has not fulfilled his duty

row.title: Ibn Kathir
sub: the raising has not come yet

then: Ibn Jarir said the disbeliever {trap}claims he has fulfilled Allah's right upon him{/trap}, but he has not. Ibn Kathir adds another view: Allah has not yet resurrected them, {idea}until the time of humanity's earthly life is complete.{/idea}
now: You tick off your prayers and charity like a checklist and feel you are basically square with Allah. {trap}The feeling of being done is the danger.{/trap} There is still time left on the clock.
old: I have done enough. Allah and I are even.
new: I have not yet done all I was asked, and there is still time to do more.
try: Pick one duty you have been doing half-way, and do it fully once today.

title: Look at your plate.
subtitle: Food as a sign and a favor
then: Ibn Kathir says this is {reward}a call to reflect upon Allah's favor.{/reward} It is also evidence: {idea}vegetation coming to life from lifeless earth{/idea} shows bodies can be brought back after becoming dust.
now: You eat lunch at your desk while answering messages and could not say afterwards what it was. {idea}The verse says: stop and look at it.{/idea} Rice, bread, an apple. Each one came up out of dead ground.
old: Food is just fuel I grab between tasks.
new: Every meal is a gift and a quiet proof that life returns.
try: At your next meal, look at your food for ten seconds before eating, and say bismillah slowly.

title: It starts with water poured from the sky.
subtitle: The first step behind every meal
then: Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: {idea}We sent it down from the sky to the earth.{/idea} After calling man to look at his food, the verse goes back to the start of the chain. {reward}Every meal begins with rain.{/reward}
now: You leave the tap running while brushing your teeth. You complain when it rains on your commute. {reward}That same rain is in your breakfast.{/reward}
old: Rain is mostly an inconvenience.
new: Rain is Allah pouring out the first step of my provision.
try: The next time it rains, say a short thank you instead of a complaint.

title: Then the ground splits open.
subtitle: Hard earth giving way to life
then: Ibn Kathir describes it: the water enters the earth and {idea}mingles with the parts of the seeds that are left in it.{/idea} From this {reward}the seeds grow, rise up and appear on the surface.{/reward}
now: You walk past a crack in the pavement and a green shoot is pushing through. {idea}Something soft beat something hard.{/idea} Your heart can feel like that pavement some weeks. It can still open.
old: Some things are too hard and closed to ever change.
new: Allah splits open what looks sealed, even the earth.
try: Look for one green thing growing in an unlikely place today and pause on it.

title: Grain, the quiet base of every table.
subtitle: Seeds that feed the world
then: Ibn Kathir says {reward}al-Habb refers to all types of seeds or grains.{/reward} The verse says Allah caused them to grow. The farmer plants, but {idea}the growing belongs to Him.{/idea}
now: Bread at breakfast, rice at dinner, pasta for the kids. {reward}Grain is in almost every meal you eat.{/reward} You have never once made a seed sprout by yourself.
old: Bread comes from the shop.
new: Every grain I eat was grown by Allah from the dead ground.
try: Do not waste any bread or rice today. Finish it or save it.

title: Grapes for you, green fodder for the animals.
subtitle: Provision for people and livestock alike
then: Ibn Kathir says grapes are well known, and {reward}al-Qadb are the moist green plants that animals graze on.{/reward} Al-Hasan al-Basri said it is fodder. {idea}The same rain feeds your fruit and the animals' grass.{/idea}
now: You buy grapes at the market. The milk in your fridge came from a cow that ate grass. {idea}Both were on Allah's list.{/idea} Your food chain is longer than you think.
old: My food has nothing to do with animals in a field.
new: Allah feeds me and the animals that feed me, from the same earth.
try: Feed a bird or animal today, or put out water for one.

title: Olives and dates, food and oil and sweetness.
subtitle: Trees that give in many ways
then: Ibn Kathir notes the olive {reward}is a food just as its juice is a food{/reward}, eaten at breakfast and used as oil. Dates are eaten unripe, ripe and dried, and {idea}their juice is made into drinks and vinegar.{/idea}
now: Olive oil in the pan, a date to open your fast, a jar of olives in the fridge door. {reward}One tree keeps giving in ways you stopped noticing.{/reward}
old: These are just ordinary foods in my kitchen.
new: Each tree Allah grows gives me provision in many forms.
try: Eat one date or a spoon of olive oil today and thank Allah for the tree it came from.

title: Gardens thick with trees.
subtitle: Abundance gathered in one place
then: Al-Hasan and Qatadah said {reward}ghulb are gardens of date palms that are thick and handsome.{/reward} Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said it means everything that is gathered and collected. {idea}Allah did not give just enough. He gave thick gardens.{/idea}
now: You walk through a park in spring, every tree heavy with leaves, while thinking about your overdraft. {reward}Abundance is all around you.{/reward} It is easy to see only what is missing.
old: Allah gives me just barely what I need.
new: Allah's provision is dense and generous, more than I notice.
try: Spend five minutes outside near trees today without your phone.

title: Fruit, and grass, and the humility to not know.
subtitle: Even the companions paused on a word

row.title: Abu Bakr's caution
sub: I will not say what I do not know

then: Ibn Abbas said abb is what grazing animals eat. Abu Bakr, asked about it, said: {idea}what sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I said about the Book of Allah that which I did not know.{/idea} Umar reflected on the same word.
now: Someone in the group chat asks what a verse means and you are tempted to type a confident answer you half-remember. {idea}Abu Bakr would have stayed quiet.{/idea} I do not know is an honorable reply.
old: I should always have an answer when someone asks about religion.
new: Saying I do not know about Allah's Book is a form of respect.
try: The next time you are unsure about a religious question, say so and offer to find out.

title: All of it, for you and your animals.
subtitle: The purpose of the whole list
then: After the list of crops, the verse names the purpose: {reward}provision and benefit for you and your cattle.{/reward} Ibn Kathir framed the whole passage as a reply {idea}against whoever denies life after death.{/idea}
now: You open the fridge and say there is nothing to eat. It is full. {reward}All of that was arranged for you{/reward}, down to the grass that fed the animal behind your yogurt.
old: I earned the food in my house, so it is simply mine.
new: Everything I eat was laid out by Allah as a gift and a sign.
try: Say a full grace before and after one meal today, slowly.

title: Then comes the Deafening Blast.
subtitle: A name for the Day that pierces hearing
then: Ibn Abbas said {trap}As-Sakhkhah is one of the names of the Day of Judgement{/trap} that Allah magnified and warned of. Al-Baghawi said it is called this because {idea}it will deafen the ears.{/idea} The talk of gardens ends abruptly.
now: You wear noise-cancelling headphones on the train so nothing reaches you. {idea}One sound will reach everyone.{/idea} The verse is a gentle shake while there is still quiet to prepare in.
old: The Day of Judgement is far off and easy to tune out.
new: A sound is coming that no one can tune out, so I can prepare now.
try: Sit in silence for two minutes today and think about one thing you want to fix before that Day.

title: You will run even from your brother.
subtitle: The bond you trusted, set aside

row.title: his brother
sub: the one who had his back

then: Ibn Kathir says a man {trap}will see them and then flee from them{/trap}, because the horror is so great. Even the great Messengers will say, O myself, on that Day, asking only for themselves.
now: Your brother bails you out of debt, drives you to the airport, covers for you with your parents. {idea}On that Day he will be running too.{/idea} So the best thing you can do for each other is now.
old: My brother will always be able to help me.
new: On that Day even my brother cannot carry me, so we help each other toward good now.
try: Message a sibling or close friend today and remind them of one good thing, gently.

title: And from his mother and his father.
subtitle: The closest love will not hold you
then: Qatadah explained the order: {trap}the most beloved and then the next most beloved, the closest of kin and then the next closest{/trap}, all due to the terror of that Day. Ibn Kathir notes even Isa will not ask for Maryam.
now: You still call your mother when things go wrong, even at forty. {idea}That Day you will face it without her.{/idea} The verse is not cold. It pushes you to honor her while you can.
old: My parents' love will somehow cover for me.
new: No one's love can stand in for my own account, so I serve my parents now.
try: Call or visit a parent today, or make dua for them if they have passed.

title: And from his wife and his children.
subtitle: The family you worked for
then: Ibn Kathir explains a man will flee from them all {trap}because the horror will be so great and the matter so weighty.{/trap} The list moves from brother to parents to spouse and children, {idea}the very people one lives for.{/idea}
now: You work late every night, telling yourself it is all for the family. {idea}Ask what you are actually giving them that lasts.{/idea} A full bank account, or a home where Allah is remembered.
old: Everything I do for my family will protect me.
new: My family is a trust I answer for, not a shield I hide behind.
try: Do one small act of worship with your family today, even a shared dua at dinner.

title: Each person, busy enough with their own case.
subtitle: Too occupied to look at anyone else
then: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that people will be gathered {trap}barefoot and naked.{/trap} When a woman asked if they would see each other, the Prophet ﷺ answered with this verse: {idea}each will be too busy to look.{/idea}
now: You spend twenty minutes reading about someone else's scandal online. {idea}On that Day no one will have a second to spare for anyone else's file.{/idea} That makes today's time for your own heart precious.
old: Keeping track of other people's faults is harmless.
new: My own account is all I will have time for, so I start on it now.
try: Skip one piece of gossip today, online or in person, and spend that time on your own prayer.

title: Some faces will be shining that Day.
subtitle: The people of Paradise, seen at once
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}the people will be divided into two parties.{/idea} Some faces will be musfirah, {reward}which means bright.{/reward} These are the people of Paradise. After all the fleeing, hope appears.
now: You spend time in front of the mirror before work. {idea}There is a brightness no product gives.{/idea} It is being built every time you choose good when no one is watching.
old: How I look is mostly about my appearance.
new: The face that will shine is shaped by the heart and deeds behind it.
try: Do one good deed today that no one will ever know about.

title: Laughing, with good news written on them.
subtitle: Joy that cannot be hidden
then: Ibn Kathir explains these faces are {reward}happy and pleased due to the joy in their hearts.{/reward} {idea}The good news will be apparent on their faces.{/idea} In the middle of a terrifying Day, there is laughter.
now: You remember the moment you got the job offer, or the call that the surgery went well. You could not stop smiling. {reward}That is a small taste of what the verse describes.{/reward}
old: Religion is mostly about fear and seriousness.
new: The end Allah offers the faithful is laughter and good news.
try: Tell someone one piece of good news today, and smile while you do it.

title: Other faces, covered in dust.
subtitle: The second group on that Day
then: Right after the bright faces, the verse shows the other party: {trap}faces that Day will be dust-stained.{/trap} Ibn Kathir presents the two groups side by side. {idea}The same Day, two very different faces.{/idea}
now: You come home after a long day of small lies and short tempers, and you feel grimy inside. {idea}That feeling is a warning, not a verdict.{/idea} A sincere tawbah can wash it tonight.
old: The dust of my wrong choices just stays on me.
new: While I am alive, I can still wash my face clean with repentance.
try: Before sleeping tonight, ask Allah's forgiveness for one specific thing from today.

title: Darkness settles over them.
subtitle: Gloom that overcomes the face
then: Ibn Abbas said {trap}this means that the faces will be overcome with darkness.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains qatarah simply as darkness. {idea}It is the opposite of the light described a few verses earlier.{/idea}
now: Some evenings you feel a heaviness after a day spent ignoring what you know is right. {idea}You have time to turn on a light.{/idea} Two rakah in a dim room can change the mood of a whole night.
old: The darkness I feel inside is just how I am.
new: Darkness is what happens without Allah's light, and I can turn back to it now.
try: Pray two extra rakah tonight and ask Allah for light in your heart.

title: Denial in the heart, wrongdoing in the hands.
subtitle: Who the dusty faces belong to
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}they are disbelievers in their hearts, evildoers in their actions.{/trap} He links it to 71:27. The surah that began with a frown at a sincere man ends by showing {idea}what the heart holds always reaches the face.{/idea}
now: Notice where your private thoughts and your daily habits line up. {idea}What you believe quietly becomes what you do loudly.{/idea} That is true for good as much as for bad.
old: What I believe inside and what I do are separate.
new: My heart and my actions shape each other, and both show on that Day.
try: Pick one belief about Allah you hold, and do one action today that matches it.
